reading.p: St. Luke was not among the original twelve apostles of Jesus. He is believed to have been a Gentile convert. He was a physician, for Colossians 4:14 refers to him as "the beloved physician."

Luke was a close companion of St. Paul, traveling with him on his missionary journeys and serving as one of Paul's most trusted followers. In one of Paul's letters he writes, "Only Luke is with me." Luke was also highly educated; his writings in Greek are among the most refined in the New Testament.

reading.h2: Saint Luke's Gospel and Its Unique Characteristics

reading.p: The Gospel of Luke is the third book in the New Testament and has several distinct themes. St. Luke provided the world with a well-researched and orderly account of Jesus Christ's ancestry, birth, and earthly life, followed by a structured narrative of His ministry that highlights key teachings and events.

list: Focus on Christ's compassion: Luke's Gospel emphasizes Jesus' love for sinners, the poor, women, and Gentiles.
A universal Gospel: Unlike Matthew, which was written for a Jewish audience, Luke presents Jesus as the Savior of all people, both Jews and Gentiles.
Emphasis on prayer and the Holy Spirit: Luke frequently mentions Jesus praying and emphasizes the work of the Holy Spirit.

reading.quote: The Spirit of the Lord is upon Me, Because He has anointed Me To preach the gospel to the poor; He has sent Me to heal the brokenhearted, To proclaim liberty to the captives And recovery of sight to the blind, To set at liberty those who are oppressed; To proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord.

list: Jesus Christ's ancestry: Found in Luke 3:23-38, tracing Jesus' lineage back to Adam (unlike Matthew, which traces it back to Abraham).
Jesus' birth and early life: The most detailed account of the Annunciation, the Nativity, and Jesus' childhood (Luke 1-2).
Jesus Christ's ministry: Unique parables and miracles, emphasizing Jesus' compassion and His inclusion of Gentiles and outcasts.

reading.quote: It seemed good to me also, having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write to you an orderly account, most excellent Theophilus.

list: The Great Catch of Fish and Calling of the First Disciples — Luke 5:1-11
Raising of the Widow's Son at Nain — Luke 7:11-16
Healing of a Crippled Woman on the Sabbath — Luke 13:10-17
Healing of a Man with Dropsy — Luke 14:1-6
Cleansing of the Ten Lepers — Luke 17:11-19
Healing of the High Priest's Servant's Ear — Luke 22:49-51

The Good Samaritan — Luke 10:25-37

reading.p: The Acts of the Apostles, also written by St. Luke, is a continuation of his Gospel. It provides a detailed account of the Great Commission, in which Jesus commands His disciples to spread the Gospel to the world.

As a close companion of St. Paul, Luke was an eyewitness to the events in Acts 13-28, accompanying Paul on many of his missionary journeys. For Acts 1-12 he likely interviewed key figures such as St. Peter and St. John to document the early Church's growth. Acts was written between 62 AD and the mid-second century.
Both the Gospel of Luke and Acts were addressed to Theophilus, a Gentile, showing Luke's intent to present a well-researched, orderly account of Christianity's beginnings.

reading.quote: The former account I made, O Theophilus, of all that Jesus began both to do and teach.

reading.p: After the martyrdom of St. Peter and St. Paul, St. Luke continued preaching in Rome and led many to Christ. Idol worshippers and non-believing Jews reported him to Emperor Nero, which led to his imprisonment. Before his capture, he entrusted his writings to a fisherman, saying they would lead him to God's way.

Nero ordered Luke's hand to be severed, but he miraculously reattached it and then separated it again, leading 276 people—including the emperor's cabinet head and wife—to believe in Christ. Enraged, Nero ordered St. Luke and the new converts to be beheaded, granting him the crown of martyrdom on the 22nd of Tahisas (December 31). His body was thrown into the sea in a sack but was later found and buried with great honor on an island by a believer.

studyGuide.overview: St. Luke, a Gentile convert, physician, and close companion of St. Paul, wrote both the third Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles, addressing them to Theophilus as orderly accounts of the faith. His Gospel uniquely emphasizes Christ's compassion for the poor and outcast, the universality of salvation, prayer, and the Holy Spirit, and contains many parables and miracles found nowhere else. He ended his life as a martyr in Rome.
keyPoints: St. Luke was a Gentile convert, a physician, and one of St. Paul's most trusted companions.
His Gospel is a well-researched, orderly account stressing Christ's compassion and a universal salvation for all peoples.
Luke uniquely traces Jesus' lineage back to Adam and gives the fullest account of the Annunciation, Nativity, and childhood.
Many parables and miracles, such as the Good Samaritan and the Prodigal Son, are found only in Luke.
Luke also wrote Acts, serving as an eyewitness for Acts 13-28 and gathering testimony for the earlier chapters.
Both works were addressed to Theophilus, a Gentile, underscoring Luke's careful, orderly purpose.
St. Luke was martyred under Nero and is commemorated on the 22nd of Tahisas (December 31).

checks: St. Luke honored as Apostle/Evangelist and martyr, consistent with Ethiopian Tewahedo veneration of the saints.
Commemoration date given in the Ethiopian calendar (22 Tahisas), faithful to the tradition.
Christ presented as Savior of all peoples; no Christological error.
Emphasis on the Holy Spirit's work given without any Filioque implication.
Miracle account of the martyrdom reported as given in the slides, treated as hagiography of a saint, not as doctrine.
